passages.text: Our father answered, ‘Do not force me to agree with you without judgment so that I may seem a truth-loving judge. If you wish to hear the truth, I am more predisposed toward your view.’ Simon said, ‘How are you predisposed when you do not know what I think?’ Our father said, ‘That is easy to know; listen to how. You promised to expose Peter as lying when he says there is one God. It is entirely clear that someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood does not, if he speaks truly, say the same thing. For if he says the same thing as the one speaking falsely, he too is lying. But if he says the opposite and proves it, then he speaks truly. You cannot, then, call the man who says there is one God a liar unless you believe there are many gods. I too say there are many gods. Since I say the same thing as you before the inquiry, I am more predisposed toward you. In this respect you have no need to be anxious about me; Peter does, since I still think the opposite of him. After your inquiry, I hope, as a truth-loving judge who has stripped off preconception, to agree with the prevailing argument.’ When our father had said this, a subdued cry of praise arose from the crowds because he had argued in this way.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the participle in a middle sense concerning false speech, since the conditional argument compares two speakers making the same supposedly false assertion. A material passive alternative is the one being falsely accused or lied about. That passive sense does not itself establish the accused person as actually false; neither reading is presented as uncontested, and the conditional remains hypothetical.
The clothing-removal image and the need to set aside a prior opinion are both retained, rather than changing the father's initial shared belief into an already completed conversion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τὸν ἕνα λέγοντα ψεύσματος ἐλέξαι ἐπαγγελλόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied print has ἐλέξαι. Convict follows the context, especially the preceding explicit ἐλέγξειν and the charge of falsehood, rather than treating the form as choosing a speaker. Normalization to ἐλέγξαι would be a proposed Greek change, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected print is claimed.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking more frequently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. Those who fashioned you appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who fashioned you appear to be two
lexical_decisions.rationale: Fashioned repeats the preceding πλάσαντός, preserving Simon's shared wording and its distinction from make in the quotation. You is understood from the preceding God who fashioned you, rather than identifying an additional created object not in the context.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything (as can be shown from many passages), would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we cannot be made to stumble either by scriptures or by anyone else; neither are we deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.

The agent is a substantivized participle, the one who tests or tempts, not a separately supplied Greek noun. The main English varies the lexical roots as tempter and testing; it does not reproduce the Greek's repeated root. A neutral, root-transparent alternative is the one who tests was testing, or the tester was testing. Tempter is chosen because the preceding act tempts toward apostasy and Peter argues against identifying the agent with an omniscient God who needs to learn. The neutral testing interpretation remains a viable lexical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

source_issues.issue: The selected image-checked print places a middle dot immediately before γραφῶν. The English translates the surviving wording without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected, no wording restored, and no OCR error or established lacuna is inferred from this apparent print feature.

passages.text: ‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

lexical_decisions.rationale: The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. Also preserves the additive καὶ but does not by itself establish other sons. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves that pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving its antecedent silently.

lexical_decisions.chosen: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first two participles share the single article ὁ, which motivates a shared-subject rendering. This differs from the repeated articles before the subsequent Emmanuel and Mighty God designations. The English preserves that grammatical pattern without independently assigning the subject a later theological identity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ᾧ πειθόμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν τὰ ψευδῆ ἐπιγινώσκομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes from the scriptures as identifying the source material in which false things are recognized. The following contrast with the scriptures' true things supports this material-source reading. A material alternative attaches the phrase to recognition as its evidentiary basis: In obedience to him, we recognize what is false from the scriptures, meaning by scriptural evidence. Neither attachment is claimed to be uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτον καὶ θεοφιλεῖ λογισμῷ ἀληθὲς ὂν δογματίσαντες οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering understands the neuter phrase ἀληθὲς ὂν as characterizing the preceding assertion about the one creator, while masculine τοῦτον identifies the God handed on. A material alternative takes ὂν substantivally as being: having affirmed this one as a true being through God-loving reasoning, the fathers handed him on to us. The supplied gender distinction is retained and disclosed, not corrected or diagnosed as OCR corruption.

source_issues.issue: The selected print has a point immediately before δὲ. The English translates the surviving words as a continuous construction, without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected or missing wording restored; the apparent print feature is not labeled an OCR error or an established lacuna.
